questions.prompt: A process that destroys or removes ALL microbial life and viruses, including endospores, is:
questions.explanation: Sterilization destroys or removes all microbial life and viruses, including endospores — usually with heat, sterilants or filtration.

why.A: Disinfection destroys most microbial life on inanimate surfaces but not endospores.
why.B: Sanitization only reduces microbes to 'safe' levels.
why.D: Antisepsis destroys most microbial life on animate (living) surfaces.

questions.prompt: These green structures are endospores. What is the 'gold standard' test for whether a chemical is a sterilant?

options.text: It kills E. coli within 10 minutes
It is safe to use on living tissue
It reduces microbes to safe levels

questions.explanation: If it can destroy an endospore, it is a sterilant. Endospores resist desiccation, UV radiation and extreme heat.

why.A: Killing vegetative cells isn't enough; endospores must be destroyed.

questions.explanation: Endospore-forming genera: Bacillus, Clostridium and Clostridioides.

why.B: These are Gram-negative rods that don't form endospores.
why.C: These cocci aren't listed as endospore formers.
why.D: These are acid-fast bacteria and fungi, not endospore formers.

questions.prompt: Bleach, concentrated iodine and formaldehyde used on a lab bench are examples of:
questions.explanation: Disinfection destroys most microbial life on inanimate surfaces. Disinfectant concentrations are toxic to tissue and they won't destroy endospores.

why.A: Antiseptics are used on living tissue at safe concentrations.
why.B: Disinfectants do not destroy endospores, so they are not sterilants.
why.C: Degerming is mechanical removal from a limited area such as skin.

questions.prompt: Antisepsis differs from disinfection because antisepsis:

options.text: Destroys endospores as well as vegetative cells
Is used on animate (living) surfaces at concentrations safe for tissue
Is used only on inanimate objects like lab benches
Mechanically scrubs microbes away rather than killing them

questions.explanation: Antisepsis uses chemical antiseptics (alcohol, iodine, hydrogen peroxide) on living tissue. Some antiseptics become disinfectants at higher concentrations.

why.A: Neither antisepsis nor disinfection destroys endospores.
why.C: That's disinfection; antisepsis is for living tissue.

questions.prompt: Soap without any additives is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Degerming mechanically removes microbes from a limited area. Soap is a natural surfactant that mechanically disrupts cell membranes.

why.A: Soap does not destroy all microbes and endospores.
why.C: Disinfectants are chemicals used on inanimate surfaces.
why.D: Soap mechanically removes microbes; it doesn't just inhibit growth.

questions.prompt: Wiping skin with an alcohol prep pad before an injection is:
questions.explanation: Skin prep uses iodine or alcohol (chemical removal) plus wiping (mechanical removal) — degerming used together with an antiseptic.

why.A: Skin can't be sterilized; most microbes are removed or destroyed.

questions.prompt: Which process reduces microbes on inanimate surfaces to 'safe' levels?
questions.explanation: Sanitization reduces microbial contamination on inanimate surfaces to safe levels. 'Sanitary' = safe for use but not free of microbes.

why.C: Degerming is mechanical removal, often from skin.

questions.explanation: '-cide' means to kill: bactericidal agents kill bacteria (excluding endospores).

why.B: Endospore destruction is sporicidal — which makes an agent a sterilant.

questions.prompt: An agent that inhibits the growth of fungi without killing them is:
questions.explanation: '-static' means to stand still: microbistatic, bacteriostatic and fungistatic agents inhibit growth.

questions.prompt: A sporicidal agent is also considered a:
questions.explanation: Sporicidal agents destroy bacterial endospores, which makes them sterilants (e.g., 2% glutaraldehyde, ethylene oxide gas).

why.A: Sanitizers only reduce microbes to safe levels.
why.B: Antiseptics must be safe on tissue and don't destroy endospores.
why.D: Sporicidal agents destroy, not just inhibit.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of a chemical sterilant?
questions.explanation: Examples of sterilants: 2% glutaraldehyde or ethylene oxide gas.

why.B: Alcohol is an antiseptic (a disinfectant at higher concentrations), not a sterilant.
why.C: At antiseptic strength it doesn't destroy endospores.

questions.explanation: Sterilization is mostly done with heat (e.g., the autoclave), sometimes with chemical sterilants or mechanical filtration.

why.A: The slides say sterilization is mostly done with heat.
why.D: Cold slows growth; it doesn't sterilize.

options.text: The growth of microorganisms in blood and other tissues
Destruction of microbes on living tissue

questions.explanation: Sepsis: microbes growing in blood and other tissues (often fatal). Asepsis: practices that prevent entry of infectious agents (e.g., aseptic technique).

questions.prompt: Which statement about disinfectants is FALSE?

options.text: They are used on inanimate objects
They do not destroy bacterial endospores
They are safe to apply directly to wounds
Some can also remove microbial toxins

questions.explanation: Disinfectant concentrations are toxic to human or animal tissue — that's why disinfectants are reserved for inanimate objects.

why.A: True — they're reserved for inanimate objects.
